rv.q: This is feminist theatre that serves justice to its case.
Some Woman boasts a strong, cheerless scenario; it’s weaker when it becomes its heroine’s cheerleader.
Anne-Marie Duff compels as a woman tormented by injustice in Helen Edmundson’s gender-political drama
The far-fetched plot turns and some underdeveloped characters undermine the powerful messages about prejudice in Helen Edmundson’s play.
Still, with so many targets for its fury, this story delivers a generalised bludgeoning, rather than a knockout blow.
Edmundson and the director Blanche McIntyre are so busy ticking off boxes about misogyny and faceless bureaucracy that they overlook the basics.
Running unbroken at just under two hours, the show is perfect.

One of the biggest stars of the evening is Rob Jones’ beautiful set design with its meticulously timed and choreographed transitions which add atmosphere and contrast to proceedings in Director Blanche McIntyre’s splendid production.
It’s a tense and engrossing evening and a wonder to spend it with Duff, the kind of actor you could watch forever.
This is a solid naturalistic drama that articulates an important social issue, but it’s a bit too didactic for my liking.
The cast do well with what they are given, but what they are given is all over the place.
Duff does her very best with the contrived material.
An interesting premise pulled down by its own weight.
It is a cathartic and chastening watch.

cn.t: Anne-Marie Duff delivers a powerhouse performance in this rage-fueled domestic thriller, but critics find Helen Edmundson's plot twists implausibly far-fetched, undermining its timely messages about misogyny and ageism.
